params.question: Why is CT not used as the default first investigation for most clinical presentations?

answers.text: CT images require several hours to reconstruct before they can be reviewed

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Modern CT scanners image the whole abdomen in seconds and reconstruction is near-instantaneous. Time is not the limiting factor.

answers.text: CT cannot differentiate between different soft-tissue types

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: CT provides excellent soft-tissue contrast through its cross-sectional reconstruction algorithm. Soft-tissue differentiation is one of CT's strengths.

answers.text: CT delivers a radiation dose 400–500 times greater than a plain chest X-ray

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. A chest X-ray delivers approximately 0.02 mSv, while a CT abdomen and pelvis delivers 8–10 mSv — a 400–500 fold increase. This dose differential is why CT is reserved for situations where its superior contrast resolution is clinically necessary.

answers.text: CT is only available at tertiary-care centres in India

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: CT is widely available across Indian hospitals. The reason it is not the default first investigation is the significantly higher radiation dose compared to plain radiography.

overallFeedback.feedback: A chest X-ray delivers approximately 0.02 mSv, while a CT abdomen delivers 8–10 mSv — a 400–500 fold increase. This large dose gap is why CT is not the default first investigation.
CT delivers 400–500 times the radiation dose of a chest X-ray, which is why plain radiography or non-ionising modalities are preferred when they can answer the clinical question.

params.question: A patient with documented severe anaphylaxis to iodinated contrast requires an MRI with contrast enhancement. Which statement about gadolinium-based contrast agents is correct?

answers.text: Gadolinium is contraindicated because it cross-reacts with iodinated agents

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Gadolinium contains no iodine. There is no cross-reactivity between iodinated and gadolinium-based contrast agents — they are chemically unrelated families.

answers.text: Gadolinium can be given safely as it contains no iodine, but renal function must be checked first

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Gadolinium is chemically unrelated to iodinated agents and carries no cross-reactivity risk. However, below an eGFR of 30, gadolinium can cause nephrogenic systemic fibrosis, a serious fibrosing skin condition.

answers.text: Gadolinium is safe to administer regardless of the patient's renal function

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Below an eGFR of 30, gadolinium can cause nephrogenic systemic fibrosis. Renal function must always be checked before gadolinium administration.

answers.text: Gadolinium should be avoided and an unenhanced MRI performed instead, as no MRI contrast agent is safe in this patient

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Gadolinium is iodine-free and safe in patients with iodinated contrast allergy. Withholding it would deprive the patient of potentially important diagnostic information.

overallFeedback.feedback: Gadolinium contains no iodine, so prior iodinated contrast allergy is not a contraindication. However, renal function must be assessed because gadolinium below an eGFR of 30 can cause nephrogenic systemic fibrosis.

Gadolinium is chemically unrelated to iodinated contrast — iodinated contrast allergy is not a contraindication. The key safety check is renal function: below an eGFR of 30, gadolinium risks nephrogenic systemic fibrosis.

interactions.label: A patient with a severe shellfish allergy must not receive iodinated contrast me

params.question: A patient with a severe shellfish allergy must not receive iodinated contrast media.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Shellfish allergy is driven by tropomyosin, a muscle protein — it has no relationship to the iodine in contrast media. A shellfish allergy does not predict contrast reactions. Always screen for prior contrast reaction history directly, not for shellfish or iodine allergy.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. Shellfish allergy is caused by tropomyosin, a muscle protein, not by iodine content. It does not predict iodinated contrast reactions. The correct pre-imaging screen is to ask about prior contrast reaction history directly.

interactions.label: Why is MRI the first-line investigation for suspected osteomyelitis rather than

params.question: Why is MRI the first-line investigation for suspected osteomyelitis rather than CT?

answers.text: MRI detects early marrow oedema and soft-tissue changes that CT misses

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Osteomyelitis begins with marrow inflammation and soft-tissue involvement. MRI's superior soft-tissue contrast reveals these early changes before cortical bone destruction becomes visible on CT or plain radiography.

CT images bone cortex very well — that is one of its strengths. However, in osteomyelitis the early pathological changes occur in the bone marrow and surrounding soft tissues, which CT depicts poorly compared to MRI.

answers.text: MRI uses sound waves, making it safer for musculoskeletal imaging

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: MRI uses magnetic fields and radiofrequency pulses, not sound waves. Sound waves are the basis of ultrasound imaging, not MRI.

answers.text: MRI is faster and more cost-effective than CT for extremity imaging

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: MRI typically takes longer and costs more than CT. It is preferred in osteomyelitis because of its superior ability to detect early marrow and soft-tissue changes, not because of speed or cost.

overallFeedback.feedback: In osteomyelitis, the earliest changes occur in bone marrow and soft tissues. MRI's superior soft-tissue contrast detects these changes before cortical destruction appears on CT or X-ray. That sensitivity is why MRI is first-line.
MRI detects early marrow oedema and soft-tissue inflammation — the earliest signs of osteomyelitis — which CT and plain radiography miss until cortical bone destruction occurs.

interactions.label: A 28-week pregnant woman is brought to the emergency department after a road tra

params.question: A 28-week pregnant woman is brought to the emergency department after a road traffic accident. Haemoperitoneum must be ruled out urgently. Which imaging study should be performed first?

answers.text: Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: CT uses ionising radiation and iodinated contrast, both of which carry risk to the foetus. It should not be first-line when a non-ionising modality can answer the clinical question.
Abdominal X-ray uses ionising radiation and has very limited sensitivity for detecting free intra-abdominal fluid. It cannot reliably rule out haemoperitoneum.
MRI is non-ionising and safe in pregnancy, but it is time-consuming. In acute trauma requiring immediate haemodynamic assessment, bedside ultrasound provides faster answers.

Correct. FAST uses sound waves with no ionising radiation, making it safe for both mother and foetus. It is performed at the bedside and detects free intra-abdominal fluid within minutes — matching both the trauma mechanism and the pregnancy.

overallFeedback.feedback: In a pregnant trauma patient, FAST (Focused Assessment with Sonography in Trauma) is first-line. It uses sound waves — no ionising radiation — and provides immediate bedside detection of haemoperitoneum, protecting both mother and foetus.
FAST combines safety (no ionising radiation for the foetus), speed (bedside, real-time), and diagnostic adequacy (detects haemoperitoneum) — the right first-line study for pregnant trauma.
